title: Tasting and off-flavors
lead: How to taste a beer, and how to tell when one’s gone wrong.

sections.name: How to taste
know: Check color and clarity against something plain.
Let it reach the whole tongue; notice the finish.

sections.name: Light and age

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Skunky from light, cardboard from age.

know: Skunky shows most in the aroma.
Old beer tastes papery, like wet cardboard.
Old beer also loses its hops.

sections.name: Two more to know
know: DMS: cooked corn; fine at low levels in light lagers.
Acetaldehyde: green apple; the beer is too young.
These are tested at the next Cicerone level.
sections.source: American Homebrewers Association, “Acceptable Off-Flavors in Beer” (homebrewersassociation.org); Cicerone blog, “Off” Flavors in Beer: The Basics (cicerone.org)

video.title: Beer School: How to taste beer like a beer judge | The Craft Beer Channel

read.bigIdea: Taste in the same order every time.
read.where: Cicerone’s order: **appearance** (color and clarity, against a plain background), **aroma**, **taste** (let the beer reach your whole tongue), **mouthfeel** (body and carbonation), then the **finish**, which carries on after you swallow. To smell, **swirl** first, then try a quick sniff or a long one.
read.mixup: Most of what we call “taste” is smell. Skip the swirl and you miss half the beer.

read.bigIdea: The hop’s home shows in the glass.
read.where: **American** hops taste **piney, citrusy, resiny** or **tropical**: think West Coast IPA. **English** hops are **earthy**, herbal and woody. **German and Czech** hops are **floral**, perfumy and **spicy**: think pilsner. Knowing which tells you what to expect from a beer before you taste it.
read.mixup: Hoppy doesn’t always mean citrus. A German pils is hoppy too, in a floral, spicy way.
read.sayIt: It’s hoppy in a citrusy, piney way.

video.title: Lightstruck - Beer sensory characteristics, causes and control factors

read.bigIdea: Two faults that come from how beer is kept.
read.where: **Lightstruck** beer smells **skunky**, sometimes described as like fresh coffee; it comes from light and can happen in minutes. **Oxidized** (stale) beer tastes **papery** or like **wet cardboard**; hop aroma fades and the malt turns honey or toffee. Age causes it and **heat** speeds it up.
read.mixup: Skunky = **light**. Cardboard = **age and heat**. Different causes, different fixes.

video.title: Beer Off-Flavors & Detecting Diacetyl - Master Cicerone® Rich Higgins Beer Lesson

read.bigIdea: Off flavors on draft usually mean the lines.
read.where: A **buttery** or **butterscotch** flavor is **diacetyl**. Yeast normally clean it up during fermentation, but bacteria in **dirty draft lines** make it too. **Sour** or **vinegar** flavors in a beer that shouldn’t be sour are bacteria as well. If a guest says a draft tastes off, **replace it** with something else and tell a manager so the lines get checked.
read.mixup: A Berliner weisse is meant to be sour. A pilsner that tastes sour is a fault.
read.sayIt: I’m sorry about that. Let me get you something else while we check the line.

video.title: Acetaldehyde - Beer sensory characteristics, causes and control factors

keyPoints.line: cooked corn: OK low in light lagers.

read.where: **DMS** tastes like **cooked or creamed corn** (at high levels, cooked cabbage). It comes from pale malt and is normally boiled off; a **low level is acceptable** in some light lagers. **Acetaldehyde** tastes like **green apple**: a normal step in fermentation that yeast clean up with time, so a lot of it means the beer is **too young**. Cicerone expects servers to know light, age and dirty lines; these two come at the next level.
read.mixup: A hint of corn in a light lager can be normal. Strong cabbage isn’t.
